content: The principles of nutrition across all stages of life were adopted during the Second International Conference on Nutrition (ICN2) in 2014. These principles were subsequently endorsed by the 136th Session of the WHO Executive Board in January 2015 and the 68th World Health Assembly in May 2015. These events called upon Member States to implement the commitments outlined in the Rome Declaration through multi-sectoral approaches. The goals of the UN Decade of Action on Nutrition (2016–2025), declared by the UN General Assembly in April 2016, emphasize increased action at national, regional, and global levels to fulfill the commitments of the Rome Declaration. This is to be achieved by implementing policy options outlined in the Framework for Action and evidence-informed programmatic actions. Additionally, these efforts align with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, particularly Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being). Target Audience This guideline is designed for a broad audience involved in the development, design, and implementation of nutrition and public health policies and programs. The intended end users include: Policymakers at national, local, and other levels. Managers and implementers of nutrition and non-communicable disease (NCD) prevention programs. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and professional societies involved in nutrition and NCD prevention programs. Health professionals across all settings. Scientists and researchers working on nutrition and NCD-related topics. Educators teaching nutrition and NCD prevention at all levels. Representatives of the food industry and related associations. Development of the Guideline This guideline was developed following the WHO evidence-informed process for guideline development, as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. Due to the complexity of the topic and the evolving evidence base, the guideline was developed over several meetings of the WHO Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) Subgroup on Diet and Health, starting in 2012. Contributors The WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety (formerly the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development) led the development of this guideline. Contributions were made by various groups, and feedback was received from stakeholders through public consultations. WHO Steering Group An internal steering group, comprising technical staff from WHO with diverse perspectives and expertise in providing scientific advice on healthy diets, guided the work. Guideline Development Group The NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health was convened to support the development of this guideline. This group included experts who had participated in previous WHO expert consultations or advisory panels, as well as others identified through open calls for experts. The group was formed with consideration for multidisciplinary expertise, representation from all WHO regions, and a balanced gender mix. Professor Shiriki Kumanyika chaired the meetings of this subgroup. External Peer Review Group External experts with diverse perspectives and relevant backgrounds were invited to review the draft guideline. They identified factual errors, commented on the clarity of language, and addressed contextual issues and implications for implementation. Systematic Review Teams Systematic review teams with expertise in both systematic review methodologies and the subject matter were identified. For example: A team from the University of East Anglia and University College London conducted a systematic review on saturated fatty acid (SFA) intake and the risk of NCDs in adults, as assessed in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). A team from Otago University, the University of Oxford, and McMaster University conducted a systematic review on SFA and trans-fatty acid (TFA) intake and the risk of NCDs in adults, as assessed in prospective observational studies. Stakeholder Feedback Two public consultations were held during the guideline development process: one during the scoping phase in 2012 and another on the draft guideline in May 2018. Stakeholders provided feedback on clarity, missing information, contextual issues, and implications for implementation. Comments were summarized, and WHO responses were posted on the WHO website. Management of Conflicts of Interest The financial and intellectual interests of all contributors, including members of the NUGAG Subgroup, external peer reviewers, and systematic review teams, were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat. Interests were declared and assessed before engagement in the guideline development process and at the start of each meeting. Evidence Gathering and Review Saturated Fatty Acids (SFA) Four systematic reviews were conducted to assess the relationship between lower SFA intake and health outcomes in adults and children: 1. A systematic review of RCTs assessing the effects of reducing SFA intake on mortality, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), and type 2 diabetes in adults. 2. A systematic review of prospective observational studies assessing associations between SFA intake and the risk of mortality, CVDs, and type 2 diabetes in adults. 3. A systematic review of RCTs and controlled feeding studies assessing the effects of replacing SFA with other nutrients on blood lipid profiles in adults. 4. A systematic review of RCTs and observational studies assessing the effects of reducing SFA intake on risk factors for CVDs, type 2 diabetes, and adverse effects on growth and development in children. Trans-Fatty Acids (TFA) Three systematic reviews were conducted to assess the relationship between lower TFA intake and health outcomes in adults and children: 1. A systematic review of prospective observational studies assessing associations between TFA intake and the risk of mortality, CVDs, and type 2 diabetes in adults. 2. A systematic review of RCTs and controlled feeding studies assessing the effects of replacing TFA with other nutrients on blood lipid profiles in adults. Key Questions and Outcomes The guideline development process focused on key questions regarding the effects of lower SFA and TFA intake on prioritized health outcomes, including: The impact of lower SFA or TFA intake compared to higher intake. The effects of SFA intake below 10% of total energy intake and TFA intake below 1% of total energy intake. The impact of replacing SFA or TFA with polyunsaturated fatty acids, monounsaturated fatty acids, carbohydrates, or protein. Priority Health Outcomes For adults, priority health outcomes included all-cause mortality, coronary heart disease, CVDs, stroke, blood lipids, and type 2 diabetes incidence. For children, outcomes included blood lipids, weight, adiposity measures, blood pressure, type 2 diabetes incidence, insulin resistance, linear growth, and potential adverse effects. Conclusion The guideline development process was comprehensive, evidence-based, and inclusive of diverse perspectives. It aimed to provide clear, actionable recommendations for reducing SFA and TFA intake to improve health outcomes globally.
